assignments.title: 13.7 Primary Source Exercise: Two Promises in 1917
assignments.html:
PRIMARY SOURCE EXERCISE
Two Promises in 1917
Wilson and Lenin, in their own words.
Exercise · 16 points · Canvas text entry
● ─ ● ● ─ ●
HOW TO WORK
Read the two lessons and the two primary sources first, and look over your notes in My Notebook. Then write your answers and submit them as the submission box below describes.
THE TASK

Read these two short passages again in their primary source pages. Wilson, April 2, 1917: “We have no selfish ends to serve. We desire no conquest, no dominion.” Lenin, April 1917: “not the slightest concession to ‘revolutionary defencism’ is permissible.”

Answer the four questions below in the Canvas text box. Aim for four to six sentences each. You will be graded on the quality of your argument, not on which answer you give.

QUESTIONS

1. What does Wilson say the United States wants from the war, and what does he say it does not want? Why would it matter in 1917 for him to say “We desire no conquest, no dominion”?

2. Wilson speaks of “the German people” and “the German Government” as two different things. What idea about who is responsible for a war does this assume, and what does it let him say?

3. Lenin refuses “the slightest concession to ‘revolutionary defencism.’” Use “Lenin, Brest-Litovsk, and the Russian Civil War” to explain how a program like this helped take Russia out of the war. Then name one other cause of Russia’s exit that Lenin did not control.

4. Choose ONE. (a) Suppose Germany had never sent the Zimmermann Telegram. (b) Suppose Germany had never let Lenin cross Germany in 1917. Explain how the war might have gone differently, and what evidence from the lessons supports your guess. Then say what makes your guess uncertain.

GRADING RUBRIC (16 pts)

MODULE INTRODUCTION
Module Introduction: 1917: America In, Russia Out
Survey · 3 questions · not graded
● ─ ● ● ─ ●
Before you start

Welcome to 1917: America In, Russia Out. Answer the questions below before you open the first lesson. Your answers help your teacher see where the class is starting. This survey is not graded.

This module's goals:
  • Explain how the Zimmermann Telegram and the U-boat war drew the United States into the war.
  • Describe how Lenin took power and why Russia accepted the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk.
  • Compare what Wilson and Lenin each promised in 1917.

discussions.title: 13.8 Discussion: Did America's entry or Russia's exit change the war more?
discussions.html:
DISCUSSION
Did America’s entry or Russia’s exit change the war more?
Money and ships from the west, or a front that collapsed in the east?
Graded discussion · 10 points · one post and one reply
● ─ ● ● ─ ●
HOW TO WORK
Read the two lessons and the two primary sources first, and look over your notes in My Notebook. Then post your answer to the prompt below, and reply to one classmate.
DISCUSSION PROMPT

This week’s question: Did America’s entry or Russia’s exit change the war more?

Choose a side. Name at least one fact about America’s entry and one fact about Russia’s exit, and say which changed the war more and why.

Write 150 to 250 words. State one claim you believe is true. Then explain why, using the specific evidence named above. Keep to what the lessons and the sources show. If you are guessing, say so.

Then add one sentence on self-government. Pick one leader from either lesson and say whether he chose with a clear head or under the pressure of the moment. Give your evidence.

RESPOND TO A CLASSMATE

Reply to one classmate. Do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with a fact or decision they did not use. If not, say politely where you think it falls short, and give your reason.

GRADING RUBRIC (10 pts)
CriteriaSubstantive (full credit)Thin (partial credit)Missing (no credit)
Your claim and your reasons
